First, I'll start by defining what LLM throughput means in this context. Throughput generally refers to how many tokens the model can process per second. But there are different types: prompt throughput versus generation throughput. Prompt throughput is about how fast the model can process input prompts, while generation throughput is about how fast it can generate text. These might differ because processing a prompt could involve different operations than generating each token.

Next, the note should address why very short outputs are misleading. If a model generates very short outputs, like a few tokens, the throughput might appear artificially high because fewer tokens mean fewer computations per output. But in reality, the model's actual capability is better reflected by longer outputs where the throughput can be more accurately measured. So, short outputs might mask inefficiencies or limitations in the underlying processing.

Then, comparing different hardware configurations: CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs. Each has its own characteristics. CPUs are good for general processing but might not handle the heavy matrix operations of large models as efficiently as GPUs. GPUs are optimized for parallel processing, making them faster for certain tasks. Hybrid runs might use both, perhaps offloading some parts to GPU while others stay on CPU. The challenge is to normalize these measurements so that they're comparable. Factors like batch size, token length, and model size will affect throughput differently across these setups. So, when comparing, it's essential to consider these variables to avoid skewed results.

I should also think about how to measure these throughputs correctly. Tools like `speedtest` for LLMs might give different numbers based on the hardware. Also, the environment—like whether it's a local machine with specific specs—plays a role. For example, a GPU-only run on a machine with a high-end GPU will naturally have higher throughput than a CPU-only run on a machine with a weaker CPU.

Another point is the importance of consistent metrics. If someone reports throughput without specifying whether it's prompt or generation, or the token length, it's hard to interpret. So, best practices would include specifying these details. Also, when comparing across different setups, ensuring that the same model version, same tokenizer, and same batch settings are used would help in making a fair comparison.
